title: Hawaii Braces for Another Storm as Moke Approaches
summary:
Hawaii is facing another weather threat just days after Hurricane Lala battered the islands. Tropical Storm Moke is expected to bring additional flooding and gusty winds, according to forecasters. The storm is passing to the south of the Hawaiian islands, but it could drop up to 15 inches of rain on the Big Island and 3 to 6 inches on eastern Maui.

The National Hurricane Center warned that the rainfall "may produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides for the windward and southeast Big Island, especially in deep terrain and over areas that were recently affected by Lala." This is a serious concern because Lala, now downgraded to a tropical storm, already caused extensive damage. It dropped more than 30 inches of rain in some areas, triggering floods and mudslides that destroyed roads and bridges. Floodwaters swept through towns, lifting homes from their foundations.

More than 8,000 people were still without power as of Saturday morning, and full restoration isn't expected until Sept. 8. At least one person, a 90-year-old woman, died in a flood caused by Lala.

Hawaii Gov. Josh Green has asked the White House to declare an emergency in the wake of Lala. Hawaii County Mayor Kimo Alameda encouraged residents to prepare for another battering, saying, "Please anticipate interruptions in power and communication and hazardous road conditions."

The back-to-back storms highlight the vulnerability of island communities to extreme weather. As climate change intensifies, such events may become more frequent. For now, residents are bracing for more rain and potential damage.
why_it_matters: This story shows how weather disasters can stack up faster than communities can recover, threatening homes, schools, power and even lives. For young readers, it's a concrete example of how climate change could make storms heavier and more frequent in the coming years.

background_read: Tropical storms and hurricanes form over warm ocean water, and a storm can weaken or strengthen as it moves across the sea.
Hawaii is an island state in the Pacific Ocean, made up of volcanic islands with steep mountains that can turn heavy rain into fast-moving floods.
The National Hurricane Center is the U.S. agency that tracks these storms and issues official warnings.
Back-to-back storms are especially dangerous because the ground is already soaked, roads are damaged, and power may not have been restored before the next storm arrives.
Scientists say a warming climate can make storms wetter and stronger, increasing the risk for places like Hawaii.

perspectives.description: For weather forecasters and emergency managers, the storm warning is a chance to help people prepare before the worst arrives. Even with damage already done, early information can reduce injuries and save lives.

For people in Hawaii, another storm so soon means more fear, damaged roads, lost power, and possible loss of life. The death of a 90-year-old woman shows the human toll that comes with extreme weather.

Islands are naturally exposed to ocean storms, and their recovery can take a long time because they are small and isolated. When one storm follows another, the damage compounds and the system has to restart before it can recover.

Hawaii's experience could push leaders to invest in stronger infrastructure, faster power restoration, and better flood controls. If climate change continues to intensify storms, such back-to-back disasters may become a more common pattern that other regions will also need to prepare for.
